8.title: "deliver us"
8.hook: "deliver us" — asking for help is the whole posture
8.tomorrow: the commandment about rest, which is the one everybody breaks
8.howItsDone: Christians pray the Lord's Prayer whole, from "Our Father" to the end. Catholics usually stop at "deliver us from evil" when praying it alone, while Protestant churches usually say it through the doxology, "for thine is the kingdom," to the amen.

screen: `DAY EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one line with a condition in it: forgive us as we forgive. Your line was: let something go. Did anything loosen, even a little? Day eight.

The box too heavy to lift alone. The form that makes no sense. The night someone could have been called, and the phone got scrolled instead. Two small words, help me, can be the hardest ones to get out. Now look at how the Lord's Prayer ends. After the Father, the kingdom, the bread and the forgiving, it doesn't finish on something grand. It finishes on a request for rescue. Deliver us. For four days we've walked through this prayer one line at a time. Today is the last line, and it turns out asking for help isn't a weak ending. It's the whole posture.
screen: `THE BOX TOO HEAVY TO LIFT ALONE.` → `HOW THE PRAYER ENDS.` → `A REQUEST FOR RESCUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the line in the old King James Bible, Matthew chapter six: "And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil." Two halves. The first half has long puzzled readers. Would God lead anyone into temptation? The Greek word underneath, peirasmos, can mean a test or a trial as well as a temptation, so some readers hear it as: don't bring us to the breaking point. Keep us from the test we can't pass. The second half holds today's word. Deliver. In Greek, rhusai. It means rescue. Pull out. Drag clear. Think less of a parcel arriving, more of someone hauled out of a river. Even the last word is honest about a puzzle: the Greek can mean evil in general, or the evil one, and translations differ. Either way, the prayer ends with a hand reaching up out of the water. Then there's the ending the King James text goes on to give: for thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen. Scholars who compare the Greek copies of Matthew report that the oldest ones don't have those words. A very early Christian handbook, the Didache, has a form of them, used in prayer. Later copies of Matthew carry them. So today Catholics usually end the prayer at deliver us from evil, and at Mass the kingdom and the power come a moment later, after a short prayer by the priest. Protestants usually say it straight through to the amen. In Orthodox churches, the priest sings the closing words. Different habits, one prayer. Now look at the whole shape. Five lines, five days. A name: Father. A hope: the kingdom. A need: bread. A mess to clean up: forgive. And a rescue: deliver. It starts by looking up, and it ends with a hand held out.
screen: `PEIRASMOS — A TEST, A TRIAL.` · `RHUSAI — PULL CLEAR.` · `THE ENDING THE OLDEST COPIES LACK.` · `FIVE LINES, ONE SHAPE.` · then, large: `DELIVER US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit comfortably, and let one long breath out. Think of one thing you're carrying that's too heavy to carry alone. You don't have to fix it. Just name it, quietly. If you pray, you can say the line, deliver us from evil, and let it be the asking. If you don't, picture the one person you'd actually call, and imagine asking them. Notice what it feels like, for a moment, not to be the only one holding it. Forty-five seconds. The bell holds the time.
The Lord's Prayer, line five. Deliver us: rescue us, pull us clear. A prayer that ends by asking for help. Eighth word.
screen: `DELIVER — your 8th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: you can ask. Today, ask someone for one small thing you'd usually do alone. Directions, a hand with something, a second opinion. Let it be easy. Day eight.

9.title: the commandment about rest, which is the one everybody breaks
9.hook: the commandment about rest, which is the one everybody breaks
9.howItsDone: Christians set Sunday apart as the Lord's Day, with worship and, for some, a day of rest; some, like Seventh-day Adventists, keep the Sabbath on Saturday. Jews keep Shabbat from sundown Friday to Saturday night.

screen: `DAY NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last line of the Lord's Prayer: deliver us. A prayer that ends by asking for help. Your line was: you can ask. Did you ask for anything? Day nine.

Quick test. Name a day in the last month when you did no work at all. No email, no errands, no catching up on the laundry. Not a sick day. A day you stopped on purpose. If none comes to mind, that's today's subject. Run down the Ten Commandments and it's easy to feel you're doing fine. No stealing, no murder, a decent record overall. But one of the ten is about rest. It's longer than the one about murder. And it's the one that's easy to break without noticing, and even to brag about breaking. Today's word is that commandment.
screen: `NAME ONE DAY YOU STOPPED.` → `ONE OF THE TEN IS ABOUT REST.` → `THE ONE THAT'S EASY TO BREAK.`

segments.voice: The Sabbath. In Hebrew, shabbat, from a root that means to stop. To cease. Not to relax, exactly. To stop. Here's the commandment, in the book of Exodus, in the old King James Bible: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work." Then the seventh day is set apart. No work. And then the text does something surprising. It makes a list of who gets to rest. You, and your son and your daughter. Your servants. Your animals. Even the stranger staying in your town. Nobody is left out. The boss can't rest while the workers keep going. One day in seven, everybody puts it down. The reason Exodus gives goes back to the first page of the Bible: God made the world in six days and rested on the seventh. Rest isn't laziness. It's part of the pattern of creation. Now, Christians keep this in different ways, and it's worth knowing who does what. Jews keep the Sabbath on Saturday, from sundown Friday, and Jesus, as a Jew, kept it too. Christians came to gather on Sunday, the day they celebrate Jesus rising from the dead, and call it the Lord's Day. Some Christians, like Seventh-day Adventists, keep Saturday. Churches differ on how Sunday and the old commandment fit together. And then there's a moment in Mark's Gospel. Jesus and his friends are walking through a field on the Sabbath, his friends pick some grain as they go, and some religious teachers object. Jesus answers: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Jewish teachers said something very close to that too. The day is a gift, not a trap. Which means stopping isn't something you earn after the work is done. It's the gift itself.
screen: `SHABBAT — TO STOP.` · `EVERYBODY RESTS, EVEN THE STRANGER.` · `SATURDAY, SUNDAY: WHO KEEPS WHICH.` · `MADE FOR PEOPLE, NOT PEOPLE FOR IT.` · then, large: `STOPPING IS THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and it's the simplest one yet. Stop. Put the phone face down, or leave it where it is and take your hand off it. Let your shoulders drop. Don't plan the rest of the day. Don't review what you didn't finish. For forty-five seconds, nothing is required of you. If you pray, you can offer the stillness as a small Sabbath. If you don't, just notice what it feels like when nobody needs anything from you. The bell holds the time.
The Sabbath. Shabbat. A day to stop, made for people, given to everyone. Ninth word.
screen: `THE SABBATH — your 9th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: stop. it counts. Once today, stop in the middle of something for one full minute, without apologizing for it. That minute isn't wasted. Day nine.

10.title: the first story
10.hook: the first story; who your neighbor turns out to be
10.carry: the neighbor is whoever is in front of you
10.howItsDone: Christians read the Good Samaritan as a picture of what loving your neighbor looks like in practice. Many churches, hospitals and charities are named after it, and many Christians take it as a reason to help strangers in need.

screen: `DAY TEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sabbath. Shabbat, to stop, a day made for people. Your line was: stop. it counts. Did you manage one minute? Day ten.

You've heard the phrase. A good Samaritan stops at a car crash, and it's on the local news. There are laws named after it, and hospitals. Almost nobody who uses it knows who the Samaritans were, or why the phrase would have sounded, to the first people who heard it, almost like a contradiction. So today, the first story on this path. It starts with a question from a man who knew his Bible very well. He asks Jesus how to inherit eternal life, and they agree on the answer: love God with everything, and love your neighbor as yourself. Then the man asks the follow-up everybody quietly wants to ask. "And who is my neighbour?"
screen: `A GOOD SAMARITAN, ON THE NEWS.` → `WHO WERE THE SAMARITANS?` → `"AND WHO IS MY NEIGHBOUR?"`

segments.voice: Jesus answers with a story. It's in Luke's Gospel, chapter ten. "A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves." It's a steep, lonely road, and they strip him, beat him, and leave him half dead in the ditch. A priest comes down the road, sees him, and passes by on the other side. Then a Levite, who served in the Temple, does the same. The story never says why. People have guessed for centuries, but the text is silent, and they're characters in a story, not a verdict on anyone's faith. Jesus and the man asking him were Jews too. Then the third traveler. A Samaritan. Here's what the first listeners knew. Samaritans and Judeans were neighbors, related peoples who shared the books of Moses, but they worshipped on different mountains and had centuries of bad blood between them. Each side had its reasons, and plenty of both avoided the other. So the hero of the story comes from the people across the line. And he's the one who stops. The old King James Bible says "he had compassion on him." He bandages the wounds, pours in oil and wine, puts the man on his own animal, takes him to an inn, and pays for his stay. He even promises to cover whatever else it costs. Now the twist. The lawyer asked, who is my neighbor? Who counts? Where's the line? Jesus turns the question around: "Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?" Not who qualifies. Who acted like one. The lawyer answers, "He that shewed mercy on him." And Jesus says: "Go, and do thou likewise." Christians have heard it that way ever since. Being a neighbor isn't about who is close to you. It's about who is in front of you.
screen: `A MAN IN THE DITCH.` · `TWO PASS BY.` · `THE ONE FROM ACROSS THE LINE STOPS.` · `NOT WHO QUALIFIES. WHO ACTED.` · then, large: `GO, AND DO THOU LIKEWISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let a breath out. Think back over this week, and find one moment when someone needed something and you walked past on the other side. A text you didn't answer. A coworker who looked lost. Someone on the sidewalk. Don't beat yourself up. We all pass by. Just see the moment clearly. Now picture going back and stopping. What would stopping have looked like? If you pray, you can hold that person in prayer. If you don't, just hold them in mind. Forty-five seconds. The bell holds the time.
The Good Samaritan. The man from across the line who stopped, and turned the question from who counts to who acts. Tenth word.

segments.voice: Your line: the neighbor is whoever is in front of you. Today, when someone in front of you needs something small, stop for them. Day ten.

11.title: the father runs
11.hook: the father runs — old men didn't run
11.howItsDone: Christians read the Prodigal Son as a picture of God's welcome to anyone who returns. The Orthodox calendar names a Sunday before Lent after it, and Catholic and Orthodox teaching often connects it with confession and repentance.

screen: `DAY ELEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Good Samaritan. The man from across the line who stopped. Your line was: the neighbor is whoever is in front of you. Who was in front of you? Day eleven.

A grown son is walking up a dusty road toward the house he grew up in. He hasn't been home in a long time. He left badly. He said things. He took money that wasn't really his yet, and it's gone. Now he's broke, and he's practicing a speech in his head, the way you might rehearse a hard phone call. He's not hoping to be forgiven. He's hoping to be hired. And then, while he's still far off, before he's close enough to say a word, he sees his father, an old man, running toward him. Today's story is that run.
screen: `A SON WHO LEFT BADLY.` → `A SPEECH, REHEARSED.` → `AN OLD MAN, RUNNING.`

segments.voice: It's in Luke's Gospel, chapter fifteen, and it's usually called the Prodigal Son. Prodigal isn't in the story. It's an old word for wasteful, and the name was given later. A man has two sons. The younger one asks for his share of the inheritance now, while his father's still alive. Some readers hear in that: I wish you were already gone. The father gives it to him. The son goes off to a far country and spends every coin. Then a famine hits, and he ends up feeding pigs, hungry enough to envy what they eat. And then the King James Bible says: "when he came to himself." He rehearses his speech. I've sinned. I'm not worthy to be your son. Make me one of your hired workers. Now here's the moment. "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." Some scholars of the period point out that a dignified older man didn't run in public. The text only says he ran, and doesn't stop to explain. Had compassion is the same Greek word Luke uses for the Samaritan in yesterday's story. It means his gut turned over. The son starts the speech, and the father never lets him get to the part about being a servant. He calls for the best robe, a ring, shoes, and a feast. "For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found." But the story isn't over. The older brother, who stayed and worked, hears the party and won't go in. And the father goes out to him too, and pleads with him. The story ends there. We never find out if he goes in. Christians have long heard it as a picture of God: a father who runs to the one who left, and walks out to the one who stayed.

Now picture them seeing you from far off, and coming toward you before you've said anything. Stay with that picture. If you pray, you can hold the father's words, he was lost, and is found. The Prodigal Son. The one who wasted everything, and the father who ran to meet him anyway. Eleventh word.

12.title: "blessed are the poor in spirit"
12.hook: "blessed are the poor in spirit" — the upside-down list
12.tomorrow: agape: the word for love that isn't a feeling
12.howItsDone: Christians read the Beatitudes as a guide for daily life. In the Catholic calendar they're the Gospel reading on All Saints' Day, and in the Orthodox Divine Liturgy they're often sung.

screen: `DAY TWELVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Prodigal Son. A father running down the road, at an age when men didn't run. Your line was: you can come home. Did anyone come to mind? Day twelve.

Hashtag blessed. It turns up under the new car, the beach photo, the engagement ring. The people who seem to have it all worked out. Now a hillside in Galilee. Crowds have followed a teacher out of the towns, many of them sick. He goes up the slope and sits down, and he starts a long talk with a list. Who's blessed? And every name on his list is the one you wouldn't expect. The poor. The ones who are crying. The gentle ones who never win an argument. It's an upside-down list, and it opens what Christians call the Sermon on the Mount. Today's word is that list.
screen: `WHO GETS CALLED BLESSED?` → `A HILLSIDE. A CROWD.` → `EVERY NAME IS UNEXPECTED.`

segments.voice: They're called the Beatitudes, from the Latin word for blessed. In Matthew's Gospel, chapter five, they're usually counted as eight, and each one has the same shape: blessed are these people, because this will happen to them. The first one, in the old King James Bible: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." The second: "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted." Then the meek, who will inherit the earth. The hungry for what's right. The merciful. The pure in heart. The peacemakers. And the people hounded for doing right. Then the word itself. The Greek word Matthew uses for blessed, makarioi, wasn't a churchy word. In ordinary Greek it described the fortunate, the happy. Old poets even used it for the gods, who had nothing to worry about. So the sentence lands like this: the lucky ones are the broke ones. The lucky ones are the ones at the funeral. It's meant to make you blink. Luke's Gospel has its own version, shorter and blunter. It just says: blessed are you poor. No "in spirit" at all. Christians have long talked about that difference. Poor in money, poor in pride, or both. Either way, the list turns the ladder over. The people everyone overlooks are the ones it calls fortunate first. Jesus says it another way later in Matthew, and it became a saying: "the last shall be first, and the first last." Christians often hear the list two ways at once. As a promise to the people at the bottom: they are not forgotten. And, for some readers, as a portrait of Jesus himself.
screen: `EIGHT BLESSINGS, ONE SHAPE.` · `MAKARIOI — THE LUCKY ONES.` · `LUKE: BLESSED ARE YOU POOR.` · `THE LADDER TURNED OVER.` · then, large: `THE LAST SHALL BE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit comfortably, and let one long breath out. Now think of one person you tend to overlook. Not someone you dislike. Someone you just don't see. The person who cleans the building. The quiet one in the group chat. The neighbor you've never asked about. Hold their face in your mind for a few breaths. If you pray, you can hold them there the way you would in a prayer. If you don't, just let them be first in your mind for a little while. Forty-five seconds. The bell holds the time.
The Beatitudes. Eight blessings that start at the bottom and turn the ladder upside down. Twelfth word.

13.title: agape: the word for love that isn't a feeling
13.hook: agape: the word for love that isn't a feeling
13.carry: love is what you do when you don't feel it
13.tomorrow: why the symbol is an execution device
13.howItsDone: Christians often read 1 Corinthians 13 at weddings and funerals, and Christian teachers often describe agape as the love God shows first and asks people to show each other, in what they do more than in what they feel.

screen: `DAY THIRTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Beatitudes. The upside-down list that starts at the bottom. Your line: the last shall be first. Did you let someone go first? Day thirteen.

At a lot of weddings, there's a moment for today's reading. Someone's cousin stands up, a little nervous, and reads: love is patient, love is kind. It's on cards. On mugs. On the wall above somebody's couch. It's so familiar it sounds soft. But it wasn't written for a wedding. It was written to a church that was falling apart. People taking each other to court. Splitting into camps behind their favorite teachers. Showing off who was more spiritual. Paul had started that church, in the Greek city of Corinth, and he wrote them a letter. And in the middle of all the scolding, he stopped and wrote this. Today's word is the one he chose.
screen: `LOVE IS PATIENT, LOVE IS KIND.` → `NOT WRITTEN FOR A WEDDING.` → `WRITTEN TO A CHURCH IN A FIGHT.`

segments.voice: Love. English has one word for it. You love your mother, your dog, pizza, a song. Greek had several. Eros, the love that wants. Philia, the love between friends. And the one Paul chose here: agape. Christian teachers have long filled it with a particular meaning: love as a choice, not a mood. Love that acts for someone's good whether or not you feel warm about them. Now listen to how Paul describes it, in the King James Bible: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up." Charity. That's the old translation's word. It comes from the Latin caritas, which is related to the word for dear, even costly. Today charity sounds like a donation box, so newer Bibles say love. But the old word tells you something: this is love with its sleeves rolled up. Notice something else. In Paul's Greek, almost every line in the passage is a verb. Suffers long. Is kind. Doesn't envy. Doesn't brag. Paul isn't describing a feeling. He's describing behavior, the kind you could watch someone do. That's why it fit a church full of people who didn't like each other. He wasn't asking them to feel warm. He was asking them to be patient, and kind, and to stop showing off. He ends: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity." Christians say this is how God loves first. Another letter puts it simply: "We love him, because he first loved us." In plain terms, agape can be as small as a text sent to the friend who's been hard to be around.

14.howItsDone: Christians remember the crucifixion on Good Friday, the Friday before Easter. Catholic, Orthodox and some Protestant Christians make the sign of the cross when they pray, and churches often hold a crucifix or a plain cross at the front.

segments.voice: Two weeks. Say the second week's words with me, fast. Deliver us. The Sabbath. The Good Samaritan. The Prodigal Son. The Beatitudes. Love, the kind you do when you don't feel it. And today, the hardest one. Day fourteen.

segments.voice: On a steeple. On a necklace. Tattooed on a forearm. Hanging from a rearview mirror. The cross is everywhere, and it's easy to stop seeing it. So try a swap. A movement whose symbol was an electric chair. A tiny gold noose on a chain. It sounds unthinkable. But that's what the cross was to the people who first saw it. Not a decoration. The way Rome killed the people it wanted everyone to watch die. So why would anyone wear one? Today's word.
screen: `ON A STEEPLE. ON A NECKLACE.` → `NOW SWAP IN AN ELECTRIC CHAIR.` → `WHY WOULD ANYONE WEAR ONE?`

segments.voice: The cross. Crucifixion was how Rome executed slaves, rebels and anyone it saw as a threat to order. It was slow, and it was public on purpose, where people would see it and learn. The Gospels say Jesus was arrested at night, questioned, and handed to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor, who sentenced him. Roman soldiers carried it out. Over his head was written the charge: the King of the Jews. A mockery, and a warning. The Gospels keep a few things he said there. In Luke: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." In Mark, he cries out in Aramaic, his own language, the first line of an old psalm: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" The Gospels don't smooth that over. Some Christian readers say it's there so that anyone who has felt abandoned knows he felt it too. Then a turn in the history. Historians of early Christian art say the oldest surviving images more often show other signs: a fish, an anchor, a shepherd. On their account, the cross became the main symbol later, after Rome stopped crucifying people. But the idea was there from the start. Paul wrote that he had decided to know nothing among them "save Jesus Christ, and him crucified." Christians say something happened there that changed what the worst thing means. Churches put it in different words: a sacrifice, a rescue, love going all the way down. And they show it differently. Catholic and Orthodox churches often show the crucifix, with Jesus on it. Some Protestant churches show the cross empty. Both are saying something about that Friday: it happened, and Christians say it wasn't the end.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe out. Think of a hard thing from this year. Not the hardest. Just name it, quietly, without reliving it. Now notice one plain fact: you're still here. Something came after it, even if it's only this minute, sitting and breathing. You don't have to make it mean anything. Just hold both: it happened, and it wasn't the last thing. If you pray, you can bring it with you. Forty-five seconds. The bell holds the time.
The cross. Rome's execution, turned into the sign on the steeple. Fourteenth word. Two weeks.
